content: 1. Modifications or configuration details of the application or system should be described comprehensively, with links to the code provided if it is publicly available. If the system has been custom-coded for the program and is open-source, a link to the public repository where the code is housed would be beneficial for researchers attempting to replicate the authors’ work. 2. The hardware choices made should be described in detail, similar to the level of detail provided for infrastructure, to help future implementers understand the minimum technical functionality required for the software to perform effectively in similar deployments. 3. For example, details on modifications such as whether the devices were functionally “locked down” to restrict the use of non-study applications should be reported. 4. The technology platform used in the program implementation should be described in sufficient detail to allow replication of the work. For instance, “RapidSMS® is an open-source SMS application platform written in Python and Django. The SMS-based project was developed to track the pregnancy lifecycle, alerting health facilities, hospitals, and ambulances.” 5. The integration of the digital health intervention within existing health information systems (HIS), whether national or organizational, should be clearly explained. This includes how the intervention complements or improves existing workflows and processes or integrates with existing health promotion programs. 6. Many digital health projects have been criticized for operating in silos, independent of efforts to create or integrate with organizational or national HIS architectures. The degree to which a program is interoperable with existing systems, such as HL7, OpenMRS CIEL, or ICD-9/10, should be reported to gauge its readiness for scale-up or integration. 7. Authors should describe the specific intervention to which participants are exposed, such as SMS, voice messages, or USSD, as these choices may explain operational variability across deployments. Parameters like the intensity and frequency of interactions, duration of engagement, and timing of delivery should also be detailed. 8. For example, in a text message intervention aimed at behavior change, the structure, timing, and delivery of the message curriculum should be described. Was attention paid to the time of day? Were limits placed on the number of messages sent per week to avoid information saturation? 9. If new content was created, the process of enlisting qualified experts and the development, validation, and testing of novel content should be described. Similarly, if the intervention used existing guidelines, such as behavior recommendations or decision-support guidelines, these should be mentioned along with any adaptations made for the specific project location. 10. The authors should describe how the digital health intervention connects to and interacts with national or regional HIS. For example, “Text messages were sent using a customized text-messaging platform integrated with the institution’s immunization information system.” 11. The mode, frequency, and intensity of the digital health intervention delivery should be elaborated. For instance, “Parents of children and adolescents in the intervention group received a series of five weekly, automated text message influenza vaccine reminders.” 12. Authors should provide details on the formative research undertaken to capture user needs, define system constraints, map user workflows, and adapt communication content and technical solutions to fit the local context. If such details are available in separate manuscripts or documents, clear references should be provided. 13. The definition and recruitment of “end-users” should be clearly explained, along with an overview of the formative work undertaken to engage them in the system’s development. If end-users were not involved, this should also be explicitly mentioned. 14. User response to the digital health intervention should be assessed, and acceptance verified. This information is critical for documenting the likelihood of adoption among end-users. Feedback could include opinions about the content or user interface, perceptions of usability, access, connectivity, or other elements of the system. 15. Authors should consider who the digital health intervention will work for and who may face challenges in accessing it. Limitations of access among certain subgroups, such as those related to socioeconomic status, geographic location, education, literacy, or gender norms, should be candidly discussed. 16. Usability testing should describe how end-users engaged in the development of the intervention. For example, “Designing the system began with formative research with overweight men and women to solicit feedback about dietary behaviors, current mobile phone habits, and the type and frequency of messages helpful for weight loss.” 17. User feedback about the intervention or user satisfaction should be described. For instance, “Most telephone respondents reported that the platform was easy to use and simple, and appreciated the ability to obtain health information via mobile phone.” 18. Authors should report basic financial costs required to design, develop, start-up, and sustain implementation from the perspective of different system users over a specified time period. Ideally, these perspectives would include program, health systems, mobile network operator, and end-user costs. 19. If a full economic evaluation has been conducted, it should be reported according to the 24-item Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) statement. 20. Appropriate training, instructional materials, and competency assessment may be warranted, as digital health strategies typically require end-users to understand the scenarios of use and the relevant functionality. Authors should describe the instructional approaches deployed for end-users or justify their exclusion. 21. Authors should discuss the level of effort involved in the implementation and consider the constraints relevant to further scale-up of the intervention. This information is critical for understanding the generalizability of the implementation and making inferences about its viability beyond a controlled setting. 22. The contextual adaptability of the intervention should be described, including its appropriateness to the context and any possible adaptations. For example, “Our mobile phone-based survey apparatus may be particularly suited for conducting survey research in rural areas.” 23. Authors should provide details of the development of replicable processes deployed in a consistent manner. These may include software source code, screenshots of workflows/dashboards, flowcharts of algorithms, or examples of content developed for end-users. 24. Data security measures should be reported, including steps taken to secure personal information linked to a client’s identity, from identity fields to laboratory test results. This includes measures at the time of data collection, transmission, receipt, and storage, as well as access control measures. 25. If the digital health intervention is used to deliver health information or decision-support guidance, authors should describe whether national guidelines or another authoritative source of information has been used to populate system content. For example, if the system provides SMS-based advice to pregnant women, does the information align with evidence-informed practices and national recommendations?
